promptText: Why do senior teams deliberately keep the E2E test suite small compared to the unit/integration layers, rather than maximizing E2E coverage?
options: E2E drives a real browser against a real (or seeded) backend, making it the slowest and most flake-prone layer, so it's reserved for business-critical happy paths while cheaper layers catch the long tail
E2E tests cannot verify real user flows, only cosmetic details like colors and fonts
CI providers impose a hard limit on the number of E2E tests per repository
Unit tests provide strictly higher confidence than E2E tests in every scenario
explanation: E2E's real-browser, real-backend fidelity gives the highest confidence but at the highest cost (slow, more places to flake), so the pyramid's narrow top is a deliberate cost/confidence tradeoff, not an aesthetic choice.

promptText: What is the core architectural difference between Cypress and Playwright?
options: Cypress runs test code inside the browser in the same JS execution context as the app; Playwright runs out-of-process, driving the browser via each engine's own automation protocol
Cypress and Playwright both execute entirely inside the browser's JavaScript engine with no external process
Playwright only supports Chromium-family browsers while Cypress supports Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit equally
Cypress uses the W3C WebDriver protocol exclusively, and Playwright cannot communicate with any browser protocol
explanation: Cypress injects itself into the page and shares the app's execution context, while Playwright is a separate Node process that drives Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit through their native automation protocols — this single choice explains most practical differences between the tools.

promptText: Which selector strategy should be the default choice in a new Cypress or Playwright test suite?
options: Role and accessible-name based locators, such as cy.findByRole / page.getByRole
CSS class selectors like .btn-primary.mt-2
Positional selectors like div > div:nth-child(3) > button
data-testid attributes, used as the first choice for every element
explanation: Both tools converge on preferring role/accessible-name queries because they're coupled to user-facing meaning rather than markup structure; data-testid is an escape hatch for elements with no meaningful role, not the default.

promptText: Why is a hardcoded cy.wait(2000) or page.waitForTimeout(2000) considered an anti-pattern compared to waiting on a specific condition?
options: It is both slower on average (you always pay the full delay even if the condition was met instantly) and still flaky if the real operation takes longer than the guessed duration
It causes a memory leak in the browser process that accumulates across test runs
It disables Cypress's and Playwright's auto-waiting mechanisms globally for the rest of the test file
Fixed sleeps only work in Chromium and throw an error in Firefox and WebKit
explanation: A fixed sleep encodes a guess about timing: too short and it's flaky on a slow CI runner, too long and every run pays the tax even when the condition was already met — waiting on the actual condition is both faster in the common case and correct in the slow case.

promptText: What class of bug does visual regression testing (pixel-diffing a screenshot against a baseline) catch that a functional assertion like toBeVisible() typically misses?
options: Rendering/layout bugs — overlapping elements, broken CSS, missing backgrounds — where the DOM and accessibility tree look correct but the page appears visually broken
Network timeout errors that occur before any element is rendered
TypeScript compilation errors in the test file itself
Incorrect HTTP status codes returned by the backend API
explanation: Functional assertions check the DOM/accessibility tree, not rendered pixels, so a page can pass every toBeVisible() check while looking completely broken visually — that's exactly the gap visual regression testing closes.

promptText: Why do mature E2E suites seed and tear down test data through a direct API/database call instead of driving the UI through every setup step?
options: Driving the UI for setup on every test multiplies run time and introduces flaky-click surface unrelated to what the test is actually verifying
The UI is structurally incapable of creating any data, so an API call is the only technical option
Direct API calls are the only way to bypass the browser's same-origin policy during a test
Cypress and Playwright cannot simulate keyboard or mouse input into forms
explanation: UI-driven setup is legitimate exactly once — as the subject of the signup test itself — but using it as scaffolding for every other test multiplies both run time and the number of places a flaky click can break an otherwise-unrelated test.

promptText: A team mocks every single API endpoint in their E2E suite with cy.intercept / page.route. What is the main drawback of this approach?
options: It turns the E2E suite into a slow, flaky version of the integration suite that no longer verifies the real frontend-backend contract, which was much of E2E's original purpose
cy.intercept and page.route are fundamentally unable to stub POST requests, only GET
Mocking network requests violates the browser's same-origin policy and throws a security error
It forces every test to run in a completely different browser engine than intended
explanation: Network mocking is meant for determinism on hard-to-reproduce edge cases; mocking everything removes the real integration check E2E exists to provide, so teams typically run real E2E for critical happy paths and mock more liberally only for edge cases.

promptText: How do Cypress and Playwright differ in how teams achieve free parallel execution across CI machines?
options: Playwright has a built-in, load-balanced --shard CLI flag at no cost; Cypress needs either the paid Cypress Cloud dashboard or a manually configured CI matrix
Cypress has built-in free sharding while Playwright requires a paid enterprise license to parallelize at all
Neither tool supports splitting a suite across multiple CI machines under any configuration
Both tools require a third-party paid service before any parallel execution is possible
explanation: Playwright ships sharding as a first-class CLI feature; Cypress parallelization requires either the paid Cypress Cloud dashboard for dynamic load-balancing or manually splitting spec files across a CI matrix yourself.

promptText: Why can Playwright drive Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit through one identical API, while Cypress historically had only experimental WebKit support?
options: Playwright's out-of-process design isn't tied to being injected into a single browser's page context, so it can control fundamentally different browser engines through their own native automation protocols
WebKit does not support JavaScript execution when driven from an external Node.js process
Cypress only supports running tests in headless mode, which disqualifies WebKit entirely
Playwright ships a modified version of WebKit's rendering engine that behaves identically to Chromium
explanation: Because Playwright never depends on being injected into a single page's execution context, its out-of-process architecture can drive Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit through the same abstraction — the direct payoff of the architectural choice discussed for Cypress vs Playwright generally.

promptText: What is the real value the Page Object Model (POM) provides, and what is a common way teams over-apply it?
options: POM reduces the blast radius of a locator change to one file instead of every spec, but a deep, multi-level page-object inheritance hierarchy can become its own maintenance burden
POM makes individual test assertions execute faster by caching DOM query results across test runs
POM is a mandatory requirement for Cypress to function and tests cannot run without it
POM eliminates the need for any assertions inside test files
explanation: POM's value is mostly about maintenance cost as a suite grows — a locator change touches one page object instead of every spec — but overly deep POM hierarchies (base classes wrapping base classes) can become a second codebase to maintain, defeating the point.

promptText: A specific test consistently needs 2-3 retries to pass reliably in CI. What does this indicate, and what is the recommended response?
options: It's a signal of a real, likely reproducible race condition or data collision that should be diagnosed with trace/video artifacts and fixed, not permanently masked with retries
It means the CI machine's hardware is failing and should be immediately replaced
Retries fully and permanently resolve the underlying issue, so no further investigation is warranted
It indicates a bug in the assertion library itself rather than in the test or application
explanation: Retries are a legitimate tool for genuine, irreducible environment noise, but a test that needs retries every run is telling you something is actually racy — the healthy practice is tracking retry rate and treating a consistently-retrying test as a bug to fix.

promptText: Why are Playwright locators described as "lazy," and why does that matter for test reliability?
options: A locator doesn't find the element until it's acted on or asserted against, and it re-queries the DOM every time it's used, so it survives re-renders that would break a reference captured too early
Locators only evaluate once at the very end of the entire test run, after all actions have completed
"Lazy" means a locator is cached forever after its first successful match and never re-queries the page
Lazy locators skip all actionability checks in order to execute actions faster
explanation: A locator is a re-queryable reference, not a one-time lookup — it re-finds the element on every use, which is exactly why Playwright tests survive elements that re-render between when the locator was created and when the action runs.

promptText: A Playwright test clicks a button immediately after page.goto. The button is visible, stable, and enabled the instant the page loads, but nothing happens because its click handler is attached one tick later via a React useEffect. What does this race reveal about Playwright's auto-waiting?
options: Auto-waiting only checks the element's own readiness (attached, visible, stable, enabled, receives events) — it does not wait for arbitrary application/JS state like a handler being attached, so this race needs an explicit signal instead
Auto-waiting is fundamentally broken and this proves Playwright cannot be used reliably in production React apps
The correct fix is to always replace the assertion with page.waitForTimeout(2000) before every click
useEffect callbacks always run before the browser's first paint, so this scenario is impossible in practice
explanation: Actionability checks verify the element's own state, not whether application logic has finished wiring itself up — a button can pass every check while still being functionally inert, which is exactly the boundary of what auto-waiting covers.

promptText: A team splits their Playwright test files alphabetically across 4 CI shards, and one shard consistently takes three times longer than the others, dragging out the whole job. What is the most likely cause and fix?
options: Naive alphabetical splitting doesn't account for historical test duration, so slow tests cluster together; Playwright's own --shard flag load-balances using duration data, and Cypress Cloud's dashboard solves the equivalent problem dynamically
Playwright shards are incapable of running more than one browser engine, which always makes one shard slower
The fix is to disable auto-waiting only on the slow shard to speed it up artificially
CI machine performance is inherently random, so imbalance like this cannot be diagnosed or fixed
explanation: Manual splitting by file count or alphabetical order can produce exactly this imbalance because it ignores actual duration; Playwright's built-in sharding load-balances by historical timing data, which is why hand-rolled splitting schemes need active rebalancing.

promptText: A checkout flow redirects to a separate origin (a hosted Stripe payment page) mid-test before returning to the app. Why does this scenario concretely favor Playwright's architecture over Cypress's, beyond a generic feature checklist?
options: Cypress's in-browser model is built around a single injected iframe that assumes one origin, so crossing origins requires an explicit cy.origin() workaround, while Playwright's out-of-process design handles multi-origin navigation natively
Stripe's servers actively block all requests carrying Cypress's default user agent string
Playwright caches cross-origin cookies indefinitely while Cypress deletes them after every navigation
Only Playwright is capable of making requests over HTTPS; Cypress is restricted to plain HTTP
explanation: Because Cypress assumes a single injected iframe and origin, multi-origin flows like an OAuth or payment redirect need the explicit cy.origin() escape hatch, whereas Playwright's out-of-process automation drives multiple origins and tabs natively — a concrete, production-grounded example rather than marketing trivia.
